## 1. Safety

Read this section before operating the system. Installation, refrigerant work and electrical connection must be carried out by a certified installer. Do not open the outdoor unit casing while the system is powered; the fan can start without warning when the defrost cycle ends.

Keep at least 50 cm of clear space in front of the indoor unit and 30 cm around the outdoor unit. Never cover the outdoor unit with a tarpaulin in winter: it needs free airflow to defrost. Children must not play with the unit or the controller.

If you smell burning or hear grinding from the compressor, switch the system off at the isolator and contact your installer.

## 3. The controller

The indoor controller has a 3.5-inch display, four buttons (Mode, Up, Down, OK) and a status LED. The LED is green when the system runs normally, amber during defrost and red when an error code is shown.

Press and hold OK for three seconds to unlock the buttons. The controller locks itself again after two minutes without input.

aerotherm_hx9_manual.md::3.text:
## 4. Operating modes

**Heat.** The standard mode. The system follows the weather-compensation curve set by your installer: the colder it is outside, the warmer the water sent to the radiators or underfloor loops.

**Cool.** Available only with underfloor or fan-coil emitters. The flow temperature never drops below 18 °C, to avoid condensation on floors.

**Eco.** Lowers the target room temperature by 2 °C and caps the compressor at 70 % of its maximum speed. Use Eco at night or when the home is empty for less than three days.

**Boost.** Raises the domestic hot water cylinder to 60 °C once, using the immersion heater as well as the compressor. Boost switches itself off when the cylinder reaches temperature or after 90 minutes, whichever comes first.

**Holiday.** Holds the rooms at 10 °C for frost protection and skips hot water heating until the return date you enter.

## 5. Domestic hot water

The default cylinder temperature is 48 °C. Once a week, on Sunday at 02:00, the system runs an anti-legionella cycle that heats the cylinder to 60 °C and holds it for 30 minutes. You can move the cycle to another day in Settings → Hot water → Legionella, but you cannot switch it off from the controller.

aerotherm_hx9_manual.md::5.text:
## 6. Defrost

In cold, damp weather ice builds up on the outdoor coil. The unit detects this and reverses the refrigerant flow for two to six minutes to melt the ice. During defrost the outdoor fan stops, the status LED turns amber and you may see steam rising from the unit. This is normal. Heating output resumes automatically.

aerotherm_hx9_manual.md::6.text:
## 7. Error codes

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | Low refrigerant pressure | Switch off and call your installer. Do not reset repeatedly. |
| E2 | High discharge temperature | Check that radiator valves are open; reset once. |
| E3 | Water flow too low | Bleed the radiators and check the system pressure (1.0–2.0 bar). |
| E4 | Outdoor temperature sensor fault | Call your installer; the unit runs on a default curve meanwhile. |
| E5 | Communication lost between indoor and outdoor unit | Power-cycle both units at the isolator. |
| E7 | Defrost did not complete | Clear snow or leaves from around the outdoor unit, then reset. |
| E9 | Immersion heater overheat cut-out | Do not reset; call your installer. |

To reset an error, hold Mode and OK together for five seconds. If the same code returns within 24 hours, do not reset again.

aerotherm_hx9_manual.md::7.text:
## 8. Routine maintenance

Clean the magnetic filter on the return pipe every three months: close the two isolating valves, unscrew the cap, rinse the magnet under the tap and refit. Check the system pressure gauge monthly; top up through the filling loop if it falls below 1.0 bar.

Keep the outdoor unit clear of leaves, snow and garden furniture. Rinse the outdoor coil gently with a hose once a year, in spring. Never use a pressure washer, which bends the fins.

aerotherm_hx9_manual.md::8.text:
## 9. Annual service

Have the system serviced once a year by a certified installer. The service includes a refrigerant leak check, electrical safety checks, a check of the expansion vessel charge (1.0 bar when empty), cleaning of the condensate drain and a software update of the controller. Record each service in the log at the back of this manual.

## Maintenance intervals

- Chain: clean and lube every 300 km, or after every wet ride. Measure wear with the checker every 1,000 km; replace at 0.5 % stretch.
- Tyre pressure: 38 psi front, 42 psi rear on gravel; 50 psi both on tarmac. Top up the tubeless sealant every two months (40 ml per tyre).
- Brake pads: check thickness monthly. Replace when the pad material is under 1.5 mm. Organic pads last about 1,500 km in winter.
- Brake bleed: once a year, with mineral oil only.
- Cassette: replace every second chain.
- Headset and bottom bracket: check for play every spring.

## What is covered

We cover your contents against loss or damage caused by fire, smoke, lightning, explosion, storm, flood, escape of water or oil, theft or attempted theft, vandalism, impact, and falling trees or aerials.

Accidental damage cover includes one-off accidents such as spilling paint on a carpet you own or dropping a laptop. It does not include wear and tear, damage by pets, or damage that happens gradually.

## Abstract

Winter cover crops are promoted to improve soil health, but their effect on soil microbial communities in heavy soils is poorly documented. We compared a cereal rye and hairy vetch mixture with bare fallow over three winters in a wheat–barley–oilseed rotation on clay loam. Cover-cropped plots had 12 % higher bacterial Shannon diversity and 18 % higher potentially mineralisable nitrogen by the third season. Earthworm counts doubled. Grain yields did not differ significantly between treatments in any year. The benefits accumulated slowly: no microbial difference was detectable after the first winter.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::1.text:
## 1. Introduction

Soil microbial communities drive nutrient cycling, aggregate formation and the breakdown of crop residues. Cover crops add root exudates and residues during the months when fields would otherwise lie bare, and so may feed microbial growth. Most published trials are on sandy or silty soils in warmer climates. Clay loams drain slowly, warm late in spring and are harder to establish cover crops on, so results may not transfer.

We asked three questions: whether a rye–vetch cover changes microbial diversity and composition; whether it changes nitrogen supply to the following cash crop; and whether it affects yield.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::10.meta_json: {"section_index":10,"chunk_index":0,"heading":"3.3 Earthworms and yield","heading_level":3,"breadcrumb":"3. Results > 3.3 Earthworms and yield","total_chunks":14}
cover_crop_soil_study.md::10.text:
### 3.3 Earthworms and yield

Earthworm counts doubled in cover-cropped plots by the third autumn (from a mean of 110 to 225 per m²). Grain yields did not differ significantly in any year. In the second year, barley after cover yielded 0.3 t/ha less than after fallow, which we attribute to slow drying and late drilling on the crimped residue.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::11.text:
## 4. Discussion

The slow build-up of microbial effects matches trials on other soils, where differences emerged only after several seasons. The larger nitrogen pool suggests that, over time, fertiliser rates after cover crops could be reduced, but we did not test reduced rates. The absence of a yield gain is common in short trials; the costs of seed and establishment were not recovered in three years.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::12.text:
## 5. Limitations

This is a single-site trial on one soil type, with four replicates, so statistical power is limited. We sampled only the topsoil and only in spring. We measured potential, not actual, nitrogen supply. Weather in 2023 was unusually wet, which delayed termination by two weeks.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::13.text:
## 6. Conclusions

On clay loam, a rye–vetch winter cover raised bacterial diversity, mineralisable nitrogen and earthworm numbers within three seasons, without changing yields. Farmers should expect soil benefits to take several years and plan termination early enough to avoid late drilling.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::3.meta_json: {"section_index":3,"chunk_index":0,"heading":"2.1 Site and design","heading_level":3,"breadcrumb":"2. Methods > 2.1 Site and design","total_chunks":14}
cover_crop_soil_study.md::3.text:
### 2.1 Site and design

The trial ran from autumn 2022 to summer 2025 at a research farm on a clay-loam soil (32 % clay, pH 6.8, 3.1 % organic matter). We used a randomised complete block design with four blocks and two treatments, giving eight plots of 24 m × 12 m.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::4.text:
### 2.2 Treatments

The cover treatment was sown in mid-September each year at 60 kg/ha cereal rye and 25 kg/ha hairy vetch, drilled directly after the cash-crop harvest. It was terminated with a roller-crimper in early April, three to four weeks before drilling the spring crop. Fallow plots were kept weed-free with one glyphosate application in October. All plots received the same fertiliser: 120 kg N/ha for wheat and 90 kg N/ha for barley and oilseed rape.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::5.meta_json: {"section_index":5,"chunk_index":0,"heading":"2.3 Sampling and analysis","heading_level":3,"breadcrumb":"2. Methods > 2.3 Sampling and analysis","total_chunks":14}
cover_crop_soil_study.md::5.text:
### 2.3 Sampling and analysis

We took soil cores (0–15 cm) from each plot in late April, two weeks after termination. Microbial DNA was extracted and the bacterial 16S rRNA gene (V4 region) and fungal ITS2 region were sequenced. Potentially mineralisable nitrogen was measured by a 7-day anaerobic incubation. Earthworms were counted by hand-sorting four 25 cm × 25 cm pits per plot in October. Yields were measured with a plot combine.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::6.text:
### 2.4 Statistics

Treatments were compared with linear mixed models with block as a random effect, separately for each season. Community composition was compared with PERMANOVA on Bray–Curtis distances.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::8.meta_json: {"section_index":8,"chunk_index":0,"heading":"3.1 Microbial diversity and composition","heading_level":3,"breadcrumb":"3. Results > 3.1 Microbial diversity and composition","total_chunks":14}
cover_crop_soil_study.md::8.text:
### 3.1 Microbial diversity and composition

After the first winter, bacterial and fungal diversity did not differ between treatments. By the third season, bacterial Shannon diversity was 12 % higher under cover crops (p = 0.02); fungal diversity did not change significantly. Bacterial composition separated by treatment in seasons two and three (PERMANOVA R² = 0.21, p = 0.01), with more Acidobacteria and Verrucomicrobia under cover. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increased in relative abundance by about a third.

cover_crop_soil_study.md::9.text:
### 3.2 Nitrogen

Potentially mineralisable nitrogen was 18 % higher in cover-cropped plots in season three (p = 0.03), with a smaller, non-significant increase in season two. Soil nitrate at spring drilling was slightly lower under cover, consistent with uptake by the vetch–rye mixture.

Full-time employees receive 26 days of annual leave plus public holidays. Part-time employees receive a pro-rata amount. The leave year runs from 1 January to 31 December.

You may carry over up to five unused days into the next leave year; carried-over days must be used by 31 March or they are lost. Book leave through the HR system at least two weeks in advance for absences longer than three days. The notice period is one month during probation and three months afterwards, unless your contract says otherwise. Probation lasts six months. Unused annual leave is paid in your final salary.

If you are ill, tell your manager before 10:00 on the first day of absence. You can self-certify for up to seven calendar days; after that we need a fit note. Kestrel pays full salary for the first 20 working days of sickness absence in any rolling twelve months and statutory sick pay after that.

ledger_api_design.md::0.text:
## Goals

- Give partner integrations a stable, versioned interface to read balances and create transfers.
- Make transfer creation safe to retry.
- Keep latency under 150 ms at the 95th percentile for reads.

Non-goals: real-time streaming of balance changes (a webhook design follows separately) and bulk export, which stays on the nightly file drop.

ledger_api_design.md::1.text:
## Authentication

Clients authenticate with the OAuth 2.0 client-credentials grant. Access tokens are JWTs valid for 15 minutes; clients must refresh them before expiry rather than on a 401. Each token carries scopes: `ledger.read` for balances and history, `ledger.write` for transfers. Requests without the required scope get 403 with error code `insufficient_scope`.

Mutual TLS is required for production clients in addition to the token.

ledger_api_design.md::2.text:
## Resources

- `GET /v2/accounts/{id}` — account metadata and current balance.
- `GET /v2/accounts/{id}/entries` — ledger entries, newest first.
- `POST /v2/transfers` — create a transfer between two accounts.
- `GET /v2/transfers/{id}` — transfer status: `pending`, `settled` or `rejected`.

Amounts are integers in minor units (pence, cents) with an ISO 4217 currency code. Floating-point amounts are rejected with 422.

ledger_api_design.md::3.text:
## Pagination

List endpoints use cursor pagination. A response includes `next_cursor` when more results exist; pass it as `?cursor=` to get the next page. The default page size is 50 and the maximum is 200 (`?limit=`). Cursors expire after 24 hours. Offset pagination is not supported, because entries are inserted continuously and offsets would skip or repeat rows.

ledger_api_design.md::4.text:
## Idempotency

`POST /v2/transfers` requires an `Idempotency-Key` header (a UUID chosen by the client). The server stores the key and the response for 24 hours. A retry with the same key and the same body returns the original response with header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. A retry with the same key and a different body returns 409 `idempotency_key_reused`.

ledger_api_design.md::5.text:
## Rate limits

Each client is limited to 600 requests per minute for reads and 60 per minute for transfer creation, using a token bucket. Responses carry `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` headers. When the limit is exceeded the server answers 429 with a `Retry-After` header in seconds; clients should back off exponentially with jitter, starting at one second and capping at 32 seconds.

ledger_api_design.md::6.text:
## Errors

Errors use the RFC 9457 problem-details format, with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and a machine-readable `code`. Validation errors list each failing field under `errors`. Every response, success or failure, includes a `Request-Id` header to quote to support.

ledger_api_design.md::7.text:
## Versioning and deprecation

The major version is in the path (`/v2/`). Additive changes — new fields, new optional parameters, new endpoints — are made without a version change, so clients must ignore unknown fields. Breaking changes require a new major version. A deprecated version is supported for at least 12 months after the successor is generally available; responses from a deprecated version carry a `Sunset` header with the shutdown date.

ledger_api_design.md::8.text:
## Open questions

- Whether to offer a sandbox with synthetic balances (tracked separately).
- Whether transfer cancellation should be an endpoint or a status change.

## Week 7: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A if Av = λv for some scalar λ, the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI) = 0. An n × n matrix has n eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, possibly complex.

The algebraic multiplicity of λ is its multiplicity as a root; the geometric multiplicity is the dimension of the eigenspace, the null space of A − λI. The geometric multiplicity is at least 1 and at most the algebraic multiplicity.

Useful facts: the trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues, and the determinant equals their product. A triangular matrix has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues.

linear_algebra_notes.md::1.text:
## Week 8: Diagonalisation

A is diagonalisable if A = PDP⁻¹ with D diagonal; the columns of P are eigenvectors and the diagonal of D holds the eigenvalues. A is diagonalisable exactly when, for every eigenvalue, the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity — equivalently, when A has n linearly independent eigenvectors. A matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is always diagonalisable.

Diagonalisation makes powers easy: Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹. This is how we solved the Fibonacci recurrence in the tutorial, with eigenvalues (1 ± √5)/2.

The matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]] is the standard example of a matrix that is not diagonalisable: its only eigenvalue is 1 with algebraic multiplicity 2 but geometric multiplicity 1.

linear_algebra_notes.md::2.text:
## Week 8 (continued): Symmetric matrices

The spectral theorem: every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and can be diagonalised by an orthogonal matrix, A = QΛQᵀ. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal. A symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when all its eigenvalues are positive.

linear_algebra_notes.md::3.text:
## Week 9: Singular value decomposition

Every real m × n matrix A, square or not, has a singular value decomposition A = UΣVᵀ, where U (m × m) and V (n × n) are orthogonal and Σ is m × n with non-negative entries σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0 on its diagonal. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA. The columns of V are eigenvectors of AᵀA, and the columns of U are eigenvectors of AAᵀ.

The rank of A equals the number of non-zero singular values. Truncating the SVD to the k largest singular values gives the best rank-k approximation in both the spectral and Frobenius norms (the Eckart–Young theorem). This is the basis of image compression and of principal component analysis.

linear_algebra_notes.md::4.text:
## Week 10: Least squares

When Ax = b has no solution, the least-squares solution minimises ‖Ax − b‖. It satisfies the normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb. If A has independent columns, AᵀA is invertible and x = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb. Numerically it is better to use a QR decomposition or the SVD than to form AᵀA, which squares the condition number.

Fitting a straight line y = c + mx to data points is the standard example: each point gives one row [1, xᵢ] of A.

linear_algebra_notes.md::5.text:
## Week 10 (continued): Principal component analysis

Centre the data matrix X (subtract each column's mean). The principal directions are the right singular vectors of X, and the variance explained by component i is σᵢ² / (n − 1). Keeping the first k components gives the k-dimensional projection that preserves the most variance.

millbrook_tramways_history.txt::0.meta_json: {"section_index":0,"chunk_index":0,"heading":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","heading_level":2,"breadcrumb":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","total_chunks":6}
millbrook_tramways_history.txt::0.text:
The first trams in Millbrook were horse-drawn. In 1879 a private company, the Millbrook and District Tramway Company, laid a single line of standard-gauge track from the railway station along the High Street to the market square, a distance of a little under two miles. Two horses pulled each car, and a third was added at the foot of Castle Hill, where the gradient reached one in fourteen. The fare was twopence for the full journey and a penny for any part of it. Within five years the company was carrying nearly a million passengers a year, but it never paid a dividend: horses were expensive to feed and stable, and the company's stables on Tanner's Lane burned down twice, in 1884 and again in 1891.

In 1898 the town council bought the company under the Tramways Act and resolved to electrify the system. The council's engineer, a man named Edwin Harrow who had worked on the electric lines in Leeds, recommended overhead wires fed at 550 volts direct current from a new generating station beside the gasworks. Electrification was completed in the spring of 1902. The council ordered twenty-four double-deck cars with open tops from a builder in Preston, and extended the network to four routes: the original station line, a northern route to the cemetery and the new housing at Hill Top, an eastern route along the canal to the ironworks, and a southern route through Ashford Green to the park gates. By 1910 the network had grown to just over eleven route miles.

millbrook_tramways_history.txt::1.meta_json: {"section_index":0,"chunk_index":1,"heading":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","heading_level":2,"breadcrumb":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","total_chunks":6}
millbrook_tramways_history.txt::1.text:
The years before the First World War were the high point of the system. The trams ran from five in the morning until after eleven at night, with workmen's cars at half fare before seven. On Saturdays in summer, extra cars carried crowds to the park, where a bandstand and a boating lake had been laid out by the council partly to give the tramways something to carry. Covered top decks were fitted to most of the fleet between 1912 and 1914, after a series of letters to the local newspaper complaining about passengers arriving at work soaked by the rain.

The war brought shortages of staff and materials. Many of the conductors and some of the drivers joined the army, and from 1916 the council employed women as conductors for the first time; by 1918 more than half of the conductors were women. Maintenance was cut back and the track, much of it laid in 1901, began to wear badly. When the war ended the women conductors were dismissed to make room for returning servicemen, a decision that caused a public meeting of protest in the Corn Exchange but was not reversed.

millbrook_tramways_history.txt::2.meta_json: {"section_index":0,"chunk_index":2,"heading":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","heading_level":2,"breadcrumb":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","total_chunks":6}
millbrook_tramways_history.txt::2.text:
In the 1920s the council faced a choice. The track needed renewal at a cost the engineer put at forty thousand pounds, and private motor buses had begun to compete on the busiest routes. The council renewed the station and southern lines in 1924 and 1925, and bought eight new enclosed cars with upholstered seats, but it decided against extending the system to the new estates on the western side of the town. Instead, in 1928 it started its own motor bus service to the western estates, the first time the corporation had run buses.

The eastern route along the canal was the first to close. Traffic to the ironworks had fallen when the works went over to short-time working in 1930, and the track on the canal road was in the worst condition on the system. The last tram ran on the eastern route on the thirty-first of March 1931, and the route was taken over by buses the next morning. The northern route followed in 1934, after the council concluded that buses could climb the hill to Hill Top more cheaply than trams, whose motors overheated on the long gradient in summer.

millbrook_tramways_history.txt::3.meta_json: {"section_index":0,"chunk_index":3,"heading":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","heading_level":2,"breadcrumb":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","total_chunks":6}
millbrook_tramways_history.txt::3.text:
Trolleybuses were considered as a replacement for the remaining routes, since they could use the existing overhead power supply. A trial trolleybus ran on the southern route for three weeks in 1935 and was popular with passengers, who liked its quiet running. But the council had just signed a long contract with a bus manufacturer, and the general manager of the transport department was a firm believer in the motor bus. The trolleybus proposal was dropped in 1936.

The Second World War delayed the final closure. Fuel for buses was rationed, and the tramways, which ran on electricity from the corporation's own station, were suddenly valuable. Cars that had been stored at the Ashford Green depot were brought back into service, and the station and southern routes carried record numbers of passengers between 1941 and 1945, many of them workers at the munitions factory that had taken over the old ironworks site. Once again women were employed as conductors, and this time several also qualified as drivers.

millbrook_tramways_history.txt::4.meta_json: {"section_index":0,"chunk_index":4,"heading":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","heading_level":2,"breadcrumb":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","total_chunks":6}
millbrook_tramways_history.txt::4.text:
After the war the track and the cars were worn out, and the council voted in 1947 to replace the last two routes with buses. The southern route closed in the summer of 1949. The final tram, car number 17, ran from the station to the market square on the evening of the twenty-fourth of September 1949, decorated with flags and carrying the mayor, the general manager and a party of retired staff, among them one of the drivers who had driven horse trams in the 1890s. Several thousand people lined the High Street to watch.

Little of the system survives. Most of the track was lifted for scrap in 1950 and 1951, although a short length can still be seen in the cobbles outside the old Ashford Green depot, which is now a furniture warehouse. Car number 17 was sold to a farmer and used as a henhouse for thirty years before it was rescued by a preservation society in 1982. After a restoration that took fourteen years, it now runs on summer weekends at a transport museum about forty miles away. The original generating station beside the gasworks was demolished in 1968, but the council's tramway offices on Bridge Street, with the corporation coat of arms above the door, are now a listed building.

millbrook_tramways_history.txt::5.meta_json: {"section_index":0,"chunk_index":5,"heading":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","heading_level":2,"breadcrumb":"The Millbrook Tramways: A Short History","total_chunks":6}
millbrook_tramways_history.txt::5.text: Historians of the system have drawn two main conclusions. The first is that the council's decision not to extend the trams to the western estates in the 1920s, made to save money in the short term, left the system without any growth in traffic just as buses began to compete. The second is that the tramways shaped the town more than any other public work of the period: the housing at Hill Top and Ashford Green was built along the tram routes, and the town's main shopping streets are still the streets the trams ran along.

## Summary

Project Omega tracks the autumn movements of blue jays (Cyanocitta cristata) along the lake shore ridge. In 2025 volunteers counted 18,420 blue jays passing the ridge watch point between 1 September and 31 October, the second-highest total in the study's nine years. Peak passage was on 26 September, with 2,310 birds in four hours.

project_omega_bluejay.md::1.text:
## Methods

Counts were made from the ridge platform from sunrise for four hours on every day with suitable weather (no rain, wind under 30 km/h). Two observers counted birds flying south-west past a fixed line between two marker poles. Twelve birds were fitted with 1.2 g GPS tags in late August.

project_omega_bluejay.md::2.text:
## Findings

- Passage was strongly linked to clear mornings after a cold front: 71 % of the season's birds passed on 14 such days.
- Flocks were larger than in previous years (median 24 birds, against 15 in 2024).
- Of the twelve tagged birds, seven moved more than 150 km south-west, three stayed within 20 km of the ridge all season, and two lost their tags.
- The resident birds that stayed fed heavily on the oak crop, which was unusually large in 2025.

project_omega_bluejay.md::3.text:
## Discussion

Blue jay migration is partial and irregular: some individuals migrate in one year and stay in another. The large acorn crop may explain why a quarter of the tagged birds stayed. Next season the project will tag 20 birds and add a second watch point 30 km along the ridge.

project_omega_bluejay.md::4.text:

Thanks to the 46 volunteer counters and to the lake shore conservation trust for access to the ridge.

## Starter

The starter is a 50:50 white and wholemeal rye culture, kept at 100 % hydration.

Feeding when baking every week: discard all but 20 g, then feed 1:5:5 (20 g starter, 100 g flour, 100 g water) the evening before mixing. At 24 °C it peaks in 8–10 hours, roughly doubled, domed and smelling of yoghurt.

Between bakes the starter lives in the fridge. Feed it once a week, and give it two room-temperature feeds before baking again. If a grey liquid ("hooch") forms on top, pour it off; it means the starter is hungry, not dead.

sourdough_notebook.md::1.text:
## Basic country loaf (one large loaf)

| Ingredient | Weight | Baker's % |
|---|---|---|
| Strong white flour | 450 g | 90 % |
| Wholemeal flour | 50 g | 10 % |
| Water | 375 g | 75 % |
| Ripe starter | 100 g | 20 % |
| Salt | 10 g | 2 % |

1. Mix flour and 350 g of the water; rest for 45 minutes (autolyse).
2. Add the starter, then the salt with the remaining 25 g of water. Squeeze through until smooth.
3. Bulk ferment at 24 °C for about 5 hours, with four sets of stretch and folds in the first two hours. The dough should grow by about 50 %, be jiggly and show bubbles on the sides.
4. Pre-shape, rest 20 minutes, shape tightly and place seam-up in a floured banneton.
5. Cold retard in the fridge for 12–16 hours.
6. Bake in a preheated Dutch oven at 250 °C, lid on, for 20 minutes; then lid off at 230 °C for 22–25 minutes until deep brown. Internal temperature should be at least 96 °C.
7. Cool for at least two hours before cutting.

sourdough_notebook.md::2.text:
## Rye variation

Replace the wholemeal with 100 g dark rye and reduce the white flour to 400 g. Rye absorbs more water but builds less gluten, so keep hydration at 75 % and shorten bulk fermentation to about 4 hours. Add 1 teaspoon of caraway seeds if you like.

sourdough_notebook.md::3.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Dense crumb with big holes at the top (flying crust).** Usually underproofed. Extend bulk fermentation until the dough has grown 50 % and feels airy.

**Flat loaf that spreads.** Overproofed, or the shaping was too loose. Shorten the cold retard or build more tension when shaping.

**Pale crust.** The Dutch oven was not hot enough, or the lid stayed on too long. Preheat for a full 45 minutes.

**Very sour taste.** Long cold retards and rye make the bread more sour. For a milder loaf, use a younger starter (6 hours after feeding) and retard for only 8 hours.

**Gummy crumb.** Cut too early, or underbaked. Check the internal temperature and wait the full two hours.

sourdough_notebook.md::4.text:
## Log

- 3 May: country loaf, 5 h bulk at 23 °C, 14 h retard. Good oven spring, slightly pale — preheat longer.
- 10 May: rye variation. Tight crumb, great flavour. Bulk could have been 30 min shorter.
- 24 May: 80 % hydration test. Hard to shape, spread in the oven. Back to 75 %.

## Summary

Project Omega tracks the autumn movements of blue jays (Cyanocitta cristata) along the lake shore ridge. In 2025 volunteers counted 18,420 blue jays passing the ridge watch point between 1 September and 31 October, the second-highest total in the study's nine years. Peak passage was on 26 September, with 2,310 birds in four hours.

project_omega_bluejay.md::1.text:
## Methods

Counts were made from the ridge platform from sunrise for four hours on every day with suitable weather (no rain, wind under 30 km/h). Two observers counted birds flying south-west past a fixed line between two marker poles. Twelve birds were fitted with 1.2 g GPS tags in late August.

project_omega_bluejay.md::2.text:
## Findings

- Passage was strongly linked to clear mornings after a cold front: 71 % of the season's birds passed on 14 such days.
- Flocks were larger than in previous years (median 24 birds, against 15 in 2024).
- Of the twelve tagged birds, seven moved more than 150 km south-west, three stayed within 20 km of the ridge all season, and two lost their tags.
- The resident birds that stayed fed heavily on the oak crop, which was unusually large in 2025.

project_omega_bluejay.md::3.text:
## Discussion

Blue jay migration is partial and irregular: some individuals migrate in one year and stay in another. The large acorn crop may explain why a quarter of the tagged birds stayed. Next season the project will tag 20 birds and add a second watch point 30 km along the ridge.
